sushruta.summary: Associated with an early surgical tradition describing cataract couching, reconstructive skin grafts, and hundreds of instruments.
sushruta.note: Dating rests on the Sushruta Samhita's layers; the surviving text was revised for centuries after any historical Sushruta.

upanishads.summary: Philosophical dialogues concluding the Vedic corpus, introducing brahman, atman and rebirth, and forming the basis of Vedanta.
upanishads.note: The oldest prose Upanishads (Brihadaranyaka, Chandogya) are usually put at c. 800–500 BCE; the later verse Upanishads extend to the early centuries BCE. Individual datings vary widely between scholars.

thales.summary: Sought explanations for natural events in nature rather than in the gods, and is credited with predicting a solar eclipse.
thales.note: No contemporary record survives; the dates come from later Greek sources.

laozi.summary: The figure behind Daoism, which counsels acting in accordance with the grain of things rather than against it.
laozi.note: Possibly not a single historical person; the Daodejing may be a composite text assembled over generations.

pythagoras.summary: Founded a school that treated number and ratio as the underlying structure of reality, including the relationship between string length and musical pitch.
pythagoras.note: The man and his school are hard to separate; most attributed results may belong to followers.

buddha.summary: Founder of Buddhism, who taught a middle path between asceticism and indulgence in the Gangetic plain of the Mahajanapada era.
buddha.note: The traditional "long chronology" gives 563–483 BCE; most modern scholarship prefers a "short chronology" placing his death nearer 400 BCE.

confucius.summary: Taught that social order grows from personal character, ritual propriety and obligations running in both directions between ruler and ruled.

achaemenid-empire.summary: The first Persian empire, stretching from the Indus to the Aegean and administered through satrapies and the Royal Road.

heraclitus.summary: Held that everything is in flux and that opposites depend on each other, so stability is an appearance rather than a fact.
heraclitus.note: Known only through fragments quoted by later writers.

classical-athens.summary: The democratic city-state of Socrates, Plato, Aeschylus and the Parthenon, whose institutions and ideas shaped later European thought.
